core: A list as an abstract, ordered, resizable sequence (an ADT) with operations get(i)/set(i), add/insert, remove, and search
The dynamic (resizable) array implementation: contiguous storage, O(1) index access, amortized O(1) append, O(n) insert/delete near the front
The linked-list implementation: nodes joined by pointers, O(1) insert/delete at a known node, O(n) index access and search
A side-by-side operation-complexity comparison of the two implementations
Terminology: a Python 'list' is a dynamic array, not a linked list
supporting: What 'amortized O(1)' means for append (occasional O(n) resize, total O(n) over n appends)
Choosing an implementation from the expected access pattern (indexing vs splicing)
Head/tail pointers; singly- vs doubly-linked lists (named, not deeply taught)
outOfScope: The fixed-size contiguous primitive array and the base+i*elementSize memory-offset model (owned by the sibling 'arrays' topic; referenced in one sentence only)
Stacks (LIFO) and queues (FIFO) as their own ADTs (named, not taught)
Skip lists, unrolled lists, and other advanced list variants
Sorting/searching algorithms beyond noting linear search is O(n)

claims.claim: A list is an abstract, ordered collection of items accessible in sequence from a head to a tail; it is defined by its interface, not by any one storage layout.
The List interface supports get(i), set(i,x), add(i,x) (insert), and remove(i).
On an array-backed list (ArrayStack), get(i) and set(i,x) run in O(1) time, while add(i,x) and remove(i) run in O(1 + n - i) time because elements must be shifted.

For a dynamic array, over any sequence of m add/remove operations the total cost of growing and shrinking the backing array is O(m), so the amortized cost of resizing is O(1) per operation; append is therefore amortized O(1).
A linked list is a list implemented by each item (node) holding a link to the next item; the first node is reached from a fixed head pointer, and basic search requires linear traversal.

On a doubly-linked list, get(i), set(i,x), add(i,x), and remove(i) run in O(1 + min{i, n-i}) time; finding the node dominates the cost, and once the node is held, adding/removing/accessing takes O(1).

In CPython, the built-in list type is a dynamic array: index access (get item) and append are O(1) (amortized), while insert and delete at arbitrary positions are O(n), and 'x in s' containment search is O(n).

Appending to and popping from the end of a Python list are fast, but inserting or popping from the beginning is slow because every other element must be shifted by one, which is the behavior of an array-backed structure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is appending to a linked list O(1) or O(n)?
positions: O(1) if the list maintains a tail pointer (or you already hold the last node)
O(n) for a singly-linked list with only a head pointer, because you must traverse to the end
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Stated precisely in the lesson: insert/delete is O(1) *given a reference to the relevant node*; appending is O(1) only when a tail pointer is kept, otherwise O(n). The lesson does not claim unconditional O(1) append for linked lists.
